UPDATE: Starving Children – STENETTE

LOURENSA
Just over two years ago we travelled to rural Eastern Cape, to report on children dying, not from disease, but from hunger.

Govan: What do you do?
Nolwazi: When I'm hungry, I drink water.
Govan: For five days?

LOURENSA
We met some of the desperate mothers, struggling to feed their families.

SIPHOKAZI (2023): "I sometimes think to myself that I wish I were not alive rather than living as poor as I am."

LOURENSA
Not even local healthcare facilities could offer much hope.

SR RADEBE (2023): "I have nothing to give. My hands are tied."

LOURENSA
At the time, the only lifeline for many was feeding schemes run by the humanitarian NGO, Gift of the Givers. In 2023, they were feeding nearly 23 000 people each day.

CORENE CONRADI (2023): "I would describe malnutrition in the Eastern Cape as a disaster that requires immediate intervention."

LOURENSA It was a crisis the Eastern Cape Provincial Government was accused of downplaying, or even ignoring.

GOVAN (2023): "Do you believe this is a crisis?"
MCHUMBA: "I'll be very careful with responding with a yes or no."

LOURENSA
A 2023 report by the SA Human Rights Commission highlighted that over 100 children died in the Eastern Cape of severe acute malnutrition between April 2021 and April 2022.

LOURENSA
Then, last September the Commission demanded answers from various departments to account for the slow implementation of its recommendations, and the ongoing, and rising child deaths.

LOURENSA
This week, spokesperson for the Eastern Cape Department of Social Development, Mzukisi Solani was confident that the situation in the province is improving.

SOLANI:
"The report that we gave to the Human Rights Commission last year... we've indicated to the commission that we have stabilised. But there's still a lot of work to be done. We've stabilised because we have managed, as these different entities and departments, to pull our resources together."

Mark Heywood:
You know, I'd always be glad to hear that the crisis of malnutrition and severe acute malnutrition in children has been stabilized. But I don't know if there is evidence to support the claim that it has been stabilized.

LOURENSA
Human rights and social justice activist, Mark Heywood.

Mark
Heywood: From talking to colleagues in civil society in different parts of the Eastern Cape, the problem is not getting better.

SOLANI:
"In terms of hunger... we have been able to provide what we call community nutrition and development centres. As an example, for instance, we keep on expanding each and every year. Before the Human Rights Commission, we had 35. Now, as we speak, we've got 38."

LOURENSA
According to Solani, this amounts to one new community nutrition centre for the province annually for the past 3 years. But is this enough when data shows there was a 12% increase in child malnutrition related deaths in the Eastern Cape in 2025…

Mark Heywood:
We use the word crisis too much and we use the word disaster too much. But, you know, if children dying of hunger, within sight of shops that have food or on farms that have food is not a crisis, I don't know what a crisis is, and therefore it should be prioritized by the government.

LOURENSA
But Government claims it's being held back by a lack of money.

Solani: We are also, you know, dependent on the resources that are available. That's why we welcome, you know, the basket of other organizations that are able to come forth, you know, to assist in the work because it's not only the work of government, but it's the work of the country, and it's the work of the province.

LOURENSA
But even with intervention from NGOs and the private sector, the problem, says Haywood, is far greater than we realise.

Mark Heywood: The deaths are just the tip of the iceberg.
00:07:00:24 - 00:07:37:12
Unknown: Underneath those tragic deaths is a much larger number of children who are experiencing hunger, who are becoming malnourished, and who require - they and their families require support.
